title: Every Way to Split Into Words
statement:
You get a string s with its spaces removed, and a list words of distinct dictionary words. Put spaces back into s so that every piece is a word from the list. A word may be used any number of times.

Return every possible sentence, each written as the words joined by single spaces. Return them in any order. If s cannot be split at all, return an empty list.

examples.why: Each split point that leaves a valid rest gives its own sentence. Stopping at the first match ("ice") would miss "icecream cone".
Words can repeat, and "a aa" and "aa a" are different sentences.
Every split leaves a stray "s" at the end.

constraints: s and words[i] use lowercase English letters; all words are distinct
The answer has at most 20 000 sentences

expected: b b a b b a

hints: Decide the first word, then solve the same problem on what is left. What are the options for the first word?
Backtracking lists all sentences, but some suffixes get solved many times over. Can you cache the sentences for each starting index?
Define f(i) = all sentences for s[i..]. For each word w that s starts with at index i, prefix w to every sentence in f(i + |w|). f(n) is one empty sentence. Memoise f by i.

explain.intuition:
Every sentence starts with some word that is a prefix of s. Fix that first word, then the rest of the sentence is any split of what remains: the same problem on a shorter string. Trying every possible first word and recursing is plain backtracking, and since we must list every sentence, the output alone can be large.

The waste is in suffixes reached by different paths. In "aaaa…", the suffix at index 4 is reached by "a a a a", "aa aa", "a aa a" and more, and plain backtracking re-explores it each time. Caching the list of sentences for each start index means each suffix is solved once. It also kills the worst case: a long string that almost splits but fails at the very end ("aaa…ab") now costs polynomial time instead of exponential.
steps: Put the words in a set and note the longest word length L.
Define f(i): if i === n, return [""] (one empty sentence). If it is cached, return the cache.
For each end from i + 1 to min(n, i + L): if s.slice(i, end) is a word, then for each tail in f(end), add word or word + " " + tail to the result.
Cache and return the result. The answer is f(0).
pitfalls: Taking the first matching word greedily. "ice" matches, but so does "icecream", and both lead to sentences.
Adding a trailing or leading space when joining with an empty tail.
Returning [""] instead of [] when nothing works. Only the base case at index n is the empty sentence.

complexity.time: O(n² + size of the output) with memoisation, ignoring string copying

solutions.title: Plain backtracking
solutions.idea: Try every word that matches at the current index, recurse on the rest, and record the sentence when the end is reached.

solutions.title: Memoised sentences per suffix
solutions.idea: f(i) is the list of sentences for s[i..]. Each suffix is solved once and its list is reused by every path that reaches it.

followups: Only return how many sentences exist, for s up to 10 000 characters. What changes, and why is that easy where listing is not?
The dictionary has a million words. Would you still use a set of strings, or a trie? What does each cost per lookup?
